First, we substitute $u=1+2x.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=2\,⟹\,\frac{1}{2}\,\text{d}u=\text{d}x.
$$

Since $u\to -\infty $ when $x\to -\infty ,$ the table for the limits of integration using the rule $u=1+2x$ is as follows:

| $x$ | $-1$ | $-\infty $ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $-1$ | $-\infty $ |

So, the integral in terms of the new variable $u$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{0}\frac{6}{(1+2x)^{3}}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{-1}\frac{6}{{u}^{3}}(\frac{1}{2}\,\text{d}u) \\  & =3{\int }_{-\infty }^{-1}\frac{1}{{u}^{3}}\,\text{d}u.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we proceed by setting the lower bound equal to some parameter $a,$ integrating as usual, and then taking the limit as $a\to -\infty .$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{-1}\frac{6}{(1+2x)^{3}}\,\text{d}x & =3{\int }_{-\infty }^{-1}{u}^{-3}\,\text{d}u \\  & =3\cdot {lim}_{a\to -\infty }{\int }_{a}^{-1}{u}^{-3}\,\text{d}u \\  & =3\cdot {lim}_{a\to -\infty }{[-\frac{1}{2}{u}^{-2}]}_{a}^{-1} \\  & =-\frac{3}{2}\cdot {lim}_{a\to -\infty }{[\frac{1}{{u}^{2}}]}_{a}^{-1} \\  & =-\frac{3}{2}\cdot {lim}_{a\to -\infty }[\frac{1}{(-1)^{2}}-\frac{1}{{a}^{2}}] \\  & =-\frac{3}{2}\cdot (1-0) \\  & =-\frac{3}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$
